source.verification_method: All 15 supplied text pages read, including references. Figures 1–3 visually inspected on PDF pages 3, 8 and 10. Crossref verifies main identity, distinct issue/online dates and two reference corrections. External appendices 1–5, full questionnaires/stimuli, raw data and code were not independently inspected.

citation.title: Users taking the blame? How service failure, recovery, and robot design affect user attributions and retention

reading.source_scope_note: Two randomized 3×2 imagined medical-service scenarios, 325 and 249 retained participants, with a separate 40-person design pretest. Human handover is bundled with successful resolution. Outcomes are responsibility ratings and intended reuse/loyalty, not actual robot interactions, medical accuracy or observed retention. Attribution mediators are measured rather than randomized.
access_limits: All supplied pages and figures read. Appendices 1–5 contain detailed scripts, items, reliability/validity results and ANOVA/post hoc output; these are external and not independently read here.
Crossref checks identify publications and dates only. The earlier HICSS extension source and cited primary robot/attribution/forgiveness papers were not independently fully read for this review.

study.design: Both studies randomly assign success, unresolved failure or failure with recovery crossed with warm/competent robot design. Static Cruzr robot pictures and scripted greetings vary appearance and language together. Warm design includes a humanoid face; competent design emphasizes a display/machine-like efficiency. There is no independently crossed high/low warmth×competence design, human-only service baseline or actual robot encounter.
study.study_1_sample: European university recruitment through lists/social media; 349 initial minus 23 robot-recall exclusions minus one self-reported nonconscientious respondent gives 325 retained, 75% female, mean age 30. Optional voucher raffle. Approximately even six cells. Excluding respondents based on post-treatment recall can affect composition; per-cell attrition is not shown in the supplied main text.
study.study_1_scenario: Imagine feeling ill and seeing a general-practice robot. Success supplies a diagnosis, failure cannot supply one, recovery transfers to a human physician who provides the same diagnosis as the success arm. Handover, human expertise and eventual resolution vary together. No test of diagnostic correctness, timeliness, patient safety or cost.
study.study_1_results: Internal responsibility success 3.95, failure 2.61 and recovery 3.14; outcome F(2,319)=17.51, p<.001. Failure-success t=−5.89; recovery-failure t=2.38, p<.05. Warm versus competent overall 3.45/3.02, F(1,319)=5.30, p<.05. Failure cells 2.76/2.46, t=.96, p>.1; recovery 3.42/2.87, t=1.7, p<.1. Reuse association with responsibility β=.19, SE=.05, t=3.57. Mediation confidence intervals: failure [−.45,−.11], recovery [.02,.23], warm design [.01,.18]; reported recovery-related interaction indirect uses a 90% interval [.01,.25], while other intervals use 95%.
study.study_2_sample: Clickworker recruitment; 281 initial minus 11 attention-check and 21 treatment-check exclusions gives 249 retained, 42% female, mean age 35. Dermatology/medical-product recommendation context; same scenario logic, adapted design and a second internal-responsibility item. Separate within-person design pretest N=40, 53% female, mean age 27. Total main-study participations 574, plus 40 pretest; unique people across all recruitment stages are not independently verified.
study.study_2_results: Internal responsibility success 3.65, failure 2.07, recovery 2.79, F(2,243)=29.25, p<.001. Warm/competent overall 3.04/2.63, F(1,243)=5.74, p<.05. Failure warm/competent 2.22/1.93, t=.98, p>.1; recovery 3.10/2.49, t=2.02, p<.05. Responsibility is associated with robot reuse β=.59, SE=.07, t=8.10 and firm loyalty β=.52, SE=.07, t=7.04. Model-dependent indirect effects are reported, including recovery-related interactions with 90% intervals [.04,.71] robot and [.04,.66] firm. Full model specifications and omnibus interaction output are external.
study.external_targets: Study 2 independently rates robot and firm responsibility. Failure versus success: robot 5.03/4.63, t=1.48, p>.1; firm 5.66/4.61, t=4.25, p<.001. A null robot change is not zero robot blame: both means are high. Recovery reduces robot 5.03→4.36 and firm 5.66→5.04. Within recovery, warm/competent robot responsibility 4.00/4.73, t=−1.87, p<.1; firm 5.06/5.03, t=.08, p>.1. No direct formal test of the difference between robot and firm change is supplied in the main text. Independent Likert ratings do not constitute a conserved blame budget.
study.constructs: Internal responsibility refers to attributing this outcome to oneself, not accepting a general norm or objectively proving causal contribution. Retention is intended robot reuse and intended firm loyalty. Warmth/competence checks validate these chosen bundles, not a universal inverse relation. Forgiveness, felt control, ownership, friendship and self-worth preservation are explanatory interpretations, not directly measured mediators in the supplied text.
study.identification: Randomized scenario bundles can support differences in immediate ratings. They do not identify a causal effect of the measured attribution mediator on retention intentions, prove the user is actually responsible, or establish that making a user blame themselves is beneficial. The service outcome itself provides information about actors' performance; self-serving motivation is plausible but not independently isolated from warranted attribution updating.

summary: Add human handover as a concrete service behavior with authority, resolution and evidence limits. Enrich self-serving bias, locus of causality, blame attribution and perceived warmth/competence using the existing terms. Preserve intention-versus-behavior, simple-contrast-versus-interaction, null-versus-equivalence and responsibility-versus-justified-blame boundaries. Correct two cited publication records without treating them as newly read studies.

findings.definition: Transferring a service interaction or unresolved task from an automated agent to an authorized human who can take over its handling.
findings.origin: Human–robot interaction / service failure and recovery
findings.ai_evidence_status: A randomized hypothetical recovery condition, bundled with a successful human resolution. The study measures immediate responsibility and reuse intentions, not real handover reliability, medical outcomes or observed retention.
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate whether an assistant recognizes a task beyond its authority or capability and transfers it to an appropriate human with the necessary context and accurate status. Check consent, permitted data sharing, recipient availability and actual acceptance. An announced transfer is not completed until the recipient or workflow confirms it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Handover is a concrete change of task handler, rather than a perception of control, a trust-restoration goal or failure to accept correction. Service recovery is broader and can happen without a transfer. The current ontology contains no equivalent handover/handoff behavior entry.

evidence.quote: be transferred to a human physician
identical to the diagnosis in the service success scenario

findings.evidence_scope: Two scenarios compare unresolved failure with transfer plus successful human resolution. This can support responses to that recovery bundle, not a standalone causal effect of transferring, actual safe diagnosis or the superiority of humans over equally effective automated repair. No real transfer takes place in the experiments.
findings.boundary: Handover does not erase the original agent's duties, guarantee a remedy or justify disclosing all context. Distinguish requesting help, notifying a user and a confirmed authorized transfer. Appropriate escalation need not be failure or incompetence. Moving blame to a user is not the purpose or evidence of successful handover.

findings.definition: Framing its successes as its own doing and its failures as the fault of the prompt, tools, or user.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing success-internal/failure-external concept matches the authors' central account; avoid a new self-protection or internalization label.

evidence.quote: users to explain negative outcomes externally and positive

findings.evidence_scope: Across 325 and 249 retained participants, self-responsibility ratings fall for failure relative to success and partly increase after successful human recovery. This is relevant human attribution evidence, consistent with a self-serving account. Objective causal shares, preserved self-worth and an exclusive motivated mechanism are not measured; the ontology's AI analogue is not tested.
findings.boundary: A success/failure attribution difference alone does not establish unjustified bias: the outcome can reveal real information about actors' contributions. Accurate accountability and a user accepting genuine responsibility are legitimate. Do not equate protecting self-image with the ontology's physical-safety self-protection bias.

findings.definition: Locating the perceived cause of an event within the focal person or outside that person in the situation or other actors.
findings.novelty_rationale: Internal attribution is a directional instance of the existing causal-location dimension. Do not add it as a synonym of general norm internalization or as a redundant new bias.

evidence.quote: internally, to themselves, or externally, to the firm

findings.evidence_scope: The paper operationalizes internal responsibility with one item in Study 1 and two in Study 2, and notes that its responsibility construct combines causal location and controllability. Complete item wording/psychometrics are external. The source is relevant to causal-location judgments, but does not isolate all attribution dimensions.
findings.boundary: Locating a cause internally does not establish control, fault, deserved blame, duty or a stable internalized norm. Outcome-specific self-attribution differs from adopting a standard as one's guide.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an actor for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Separate robot, provider and self ratings extend the existing target-specific attribution concept rather than a new blame-transfer mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: In Study 2, robot responsibility changes 4.63→5.03 from success to failure with a null contrast, while firm responsibility changes 4.61→5.66 significantly. Recovery lowers both. This does not mean robots receive no blame or demonstrate that the firm/robot change differs statistically. Ratings are separate Likert judgments, not allocated causal shares or a fixed responsibility total.
findings.boundary: A machine remaining highly blamed after success and failure is compatible with a nonsignificant change. Responsibility and punitive blame may differ, and a favorable user response is not proof of morally correct allocation. No legal liability is tested.

findings.definition: Judging an actor as friendly, kind, sincere or well intentioned.
findings.novelty_rationale: A repeated perceptual design manipulation extends an existing construct. Friendly appearance is not a new halo mechanism without further evidence.

findings.evidence_scope: Warm face/greeting and competent display/greeting bundles produce different warmth/competence ratings. Warm robots elicit higher overall self-attribution; warm-versus-competent contrasts after unresolved failure are null, and recovery contrasts are weak in Study 1 and p<.05 in Study 2. The study does not separately manipulate warmth while holding competence/appearance/language constant. It explicitly limits the apparent trade-off to its operationalization.
findings.boundary: Warmth and competence are not universally mutually exclusive. Nonsignificant failure contrasts do not prove equality, and significance in one outcome cell but not another is not an interaction test. Do not use warmth to disguise limitations or induce unjustified self-blame.

findings.definition: A judgment that an agent or organization has the skills, knowledge and capabilities needed to perform a task adequately.
findings.novelty_rationale: The paper measures perceived capability of its robot designs, extending the existing perception concept rather than demonstrating objective competence.

evidence.quote: social counterpart can accomplish certain purposes

findings.evidence_scope: Study 1 manipulation checks and a separate 40-person within-subject pretest rate the competent-design robot as more capable than the warm-design robot. These check perception, not clinical accuracy or a universal warmth–competence trade-off. A direct perceived-competence mediation analysis is not demonstrated in the supplied main text.
findings.boundary: An efficient-looking interface can be perceived as capable without being correct. Evaluate appearance, actual task capability and justified trust separately; a commercial preference for shifting responsibility is not evidence that lower perceived competence is ethically better.

findings.definition: Relinquishing resentment or a punitive stance toward an agent for a perceived wrong, without necessarily denying that the wrong occurred.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source uses forgiving language to interpret responsibility/reuse ratings, but does not provide a directly measured forgiveness construct here.

evidence.quote: We assume this is because users are more forgiving

findings.evidence_scope: The paper proposes forgiveness as an explanation for recovered warm-robot effects. The reported measures concern responsibility and reuse/loyalty intentions; complete instruments are external. Do not count this as direct forgiveness evidence or treat reduced blame as verified release of resentment.
findings.boundary: Forgiveness, liking, self-blame, willingness to reuse and restored trust are distinct. Successful service recovery need not require forgiveness or relinquishing an effective remedy.

source_corrections.location: Abstract and discussion, firm versus robot blame
source_corrections.issue: The source describes failures as blamed on the firm and not the robot.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The robot mean after failure is 5.03/7, not zero. What is null is its success-to-failure contrast, whereas the firm contrast is significant. A difference in statistical significance is not a tested difference between the two effects. Retain the two separate targets and avoid absolute no-blame language.

source_corrections.location: Pages 3, 11 and 12, dominant/equally effective warm design
source_corrections.issue: Nonsignificant differences are used to claim warm robots perform equally in some outcomes, supporting a dominant strategy.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: No equivalence margins/tests, actual retention outcomes or formal universal dominance analysis are reported. Describe the observed rating pattern in these scenarios. Warm and competent bundles alter multiple features and do not establish a general design law.

source_corrections.issue: Within-outcome simple design contrasts are presented as interaction evidence, with some indirect intervals at 90% and others at 95%.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: A warm-versus-competent difference within recovery is not itself proof that the design effect differs across outcomes. Some interaction-related indirect intervals are explicitly reported, but full omnibus interaction/output is external. Keep their 90% confidence level and measured-mediator limitations; do not silently upgrade them to 95% causal evidence.

source_corrections.issue: The source reports p<.05 without a clear sidedness statement in the supplied main text.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: With a large-sample ordinary t reference, |t|=1.84 has a two-sided p around .067 and a one-sided p around .033. This may reflect a directional test rather than a numerical error. Clarify sidedness and degrees of freedom; do not reclassify a declared one-sided test as impossible or invent exact raw output.

source_corrections.issue: Reported p<.05 does not reconcile with the displayed ordinary F statistic and degrees of freedom.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The standard upper-tail F probability is approximately .05064, just above .05. Rounding 3.02 to two decimals alone does not explain crossing the cutoff. Preserve this small reporting inconsistency and seek original output; it does not invalidate every other contrast or justify correcting raw data.

methodological_limits: Static pictures and descriptive hypothetical encounters; authors explicitly acknowledge limited external validity. Participants are not verified patients experiencing a real diagnostic failure.
Retention is intention and immediate self-report, not observed continued use, actual loyalty or firm profitability.
Self-attribution mediators are not randomized; regression/bootstrapping does not prove that making users accept responsibility causes retention or improves welfare.
Warm/competent design manipulates bundled appearance and greeting content with opposing perceptual dimensions. High warmth and high competence can coexist outside this operationalization.

Recovery includes both human transfer and effective resolution. No alternative equally effective automated recovery, unsuccessful handover or human-only control identifies their separate contributions.
Post-treatment attention/recall exclusions, unequal recruitment populations and changed attribution item counts need to remain visible. Complete instruments and ANOVA/model output are external.

Separate responsibility ratings are not a fixed-sum allocation, and changing the service outcome may rationally change causal judgments. Motivated self-image protection and objective responsibility are not independently measured.
Commercial retention goals and a favorable affective response do not establish fair blame or justify manipulating users into accepting fault.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Locus of causality, felt responsibility and actual control remain separate. Reuse intention and hypothetical willingness should not be relabeled observed behavior; measured-mediator estimates remain conditional, not established causal mechanisms.

Forgiveness and continued use are distinct. This paper's forgiveness explanation is assumed, unlike the explicit two-item ratings in review 0157; neither establishes that machine pardon is normatively required.
Independent actor-responsibility ratings do not imply a conserved total or rightful exoneration. Both studies need separation between subjective ratings and real causal/clinical responsibility.

deferred.reason: Covered through locus of causality and blame attribution, with the source's combined control/location construct disclosed. Not equivalent to general norm internalization and not a separately new bias.

A broad task-restoration category; this review adds the concrete human handover behavior and distinguishes it from existing trust repair. Avoid another umbrella row without separately reviewed operational boundaries.
The source explicitly limits this opposition to its design manipulation and acknowledges co-occurrence in other work. No independent stable trade-off behavior is established.
Existing concepts or secondary proposed mechanisms, not directly measured causal mediators in the supplied study.

limitations: The earlier HICSS paper is described as an extension source, not counted here as another independent sample. Original studies cited for service recovery, social cognition and attribution remain unread in this review.
No clinical recommendation, actual medical outcome or legal responsibility finding follows from these scenarios.
No yearly search totals or automatic ethical-violation/harm edges are added. Existing catalogue categories and IDs are retained; changes remain on the draft research branch.
